newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Hebron settlers vow to stay despite pressure.
newsitem.headline: Hebron settlers vow to stay despite pressure.

text.p: Jewish settlers say "terror" has won out in Hebron but on Sunday they vowed to stay despite the deal giving most of the West Bank town to Palestinian self-rule.
"My feeling is that terror has got a victory over the state of Israel," Noam Arnon, spokesman for the 400 Jews who live amid 100,000 Palestinians in Hebron told reporters.

Anat Cohen, who like most Jews in Hebron was sitting tight in her enclave as Palestinians thronged the city welcoming Yasser Arafat, said the situation was bad but the faith that kept her in this town holy to Jews and Moslems was rock-hard.
"The Jewish people went throught the Holocaust...certainly we trust in God," said Cohen, who has lived in Hebron for 15 years.

Arnon accused Palestinians of already violating the Hebron deal with what he called "violent demonstrations" last week. On Friday, Palestinians hurled stones and handfuls of produce at Israeli soldiers during a brief confrontation near the Arab market that remains under Israeli control. No one was hurt.
He said calls by Arabs for the settlers to evacuate the 20 percent of the town Israel still occupies were "incitement to murder".
But Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, who flew into the town by helicopter on Sunday, tried to reassure Jewish settlers by saying he wanted peace.
"I tell settlers we do not want confrontation," the former guerrilla chief said, having flown to the hilltop headquarters of Israel's 30-year-long occupation that ended on Friday.
His message came a day after Jibril Rajoub, the head of Arafat's police in the West Bank, said the Jewish settlers in Hebron, most of whom carry arms, did not belong in the town.
He later defended the comment, made in a speech to Hebron residents, saying: "I said Hebron was not a natural place for these settlers and I stick by that."

The controversy highlights the problems faced despite the deal between Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The agreement leaves the 400 settlers and about 20,000 Arabs under Israeli control in the centre of the town around the tomb of biblical Abraham, which is holy to Jews and Moslems.
The rest of Hebron's 100,000 residents are policed by Palestinians but they will still rub shoulders with the settlers at key points in the city.

In the area where Jewish settlers live near Martyr's Street, which runs through the heart of the town, Israeli soldiers forced small Palestinian girl scouts to take a detour to avoid the Jewish settlers.

The 40 girls, between the ages of seven and 10 and holding little Palestinian flags, made it past two Israeli checkpoints before worried soldiers intervened to head off a possible confrontation. The soldiers pointed the girls toward the market, away from the enclaves where armed Jews live.
Under the deal that gave the Palestinians control over 80 percent of the town a wall will divide Martyr's Street to separate Jewish and Arab traffic.

"I pray to God that there will not be acts like (the) Dizengoff (street bus bombing in Tel Aviv)... and the 1,001 murderous acts that Arafat makes sure the Arabs commit against the state of Israel," said Jewish settler Cohen.
Hebron itself has been stained by Arab-Jewish bloodbaths that the passage of years has not erased.
In 1929, Arabs killed 67 Jews in Hebron, virtually ending the Jewish presence in the town until the 1967 Middle East war.
In February 1994, settler Baruch Goldstein massacred 29 Arabs at prayer at al-Ibrahimi mosque, a site sacred to Jews as well as Moslems as the burial place of the biblical Abraham.
One Arab teacher matched Cohen's fears with some of her own.
"They don't like us and we don't like them...they are bloody people. They are all Goldstein. They want to see us dead."
